title: Viota’s Monument
dek: A forest monument reached from Larkhollow: an old road, a remembered passage, and a company that chooses to preserve what it does not yet understand.

facts.Unresolved: Viota’s identity · meaning of the passage
facts.Recorded journey: 9–10 October 2026; an overnight camp is explicit

body:
Viota’s monument stands among forest ruins near Larkhollow, on the recorded route through Verdelune. The company reaches a figure covered with flowers and small carvings, then brings its writing back to someone who can read it. An investigation that begins with incomplete records ends with a name, a remembered passage and further questions.

A letter, a map and a night on the river

Ryvyt has Ilyra Bellflower’s letter when the company gathers at Emberwillow Bridge. Older Larkhollow records describe ruins hidden in the forest and a road once maintained by the village. One reminder asks that the stones not be forgotten before the next flowering. Ilyra has marked what she can on a map, but does not know what stood there or why it was abandoned.

Ryvyt, Fenwick, Saelihn and Trougar follow the river north. Six hours of travel bring them toward rugged stone as the sun sets. They make camp; the narrator describes a night passing and morning light brightening the water. Later, three companions cannot explain all their movement toward the Bell Path, while Fenwick hears a quiet tune. Their arrival is not a fully surveyed route or an uninterrupted account of every hour.

They meet Ilyra at the Petal Market, and she points out the ruins on Ryvyt’s map. Leaving the market, the company heads northeast, slightly toward the river. The monument is reached from Larkhollow’s surroundings, rather than being the bridge, the market or Hana’s distant tower.

9–10 October · reading a place before explaining it

Fenwick first notices seeds spaced at deliberate intervals along the floor. One is old enough to have fossilized in stone. Nearby carvings show a flower, fruit and an empty circle, beside another sequence continuing through seed and plant. Placing a seed in the empty circle changes nothing.

Trougar is eager to try his demolition gauntlet. Saelihn asks the others not to blast the forest, and Ryvyt insists on restraint. The narrator clarifies that the wall they are examining is not actually blocking their way. Another path leads farther into the ruins.

Saelihn’s reading of the floor suggests a former marketplace. The central figure beyond it is arranged to command attention: walls and ruins appear to honor or bear witness to her. Moss, plant carvings, rotten gathering baskets and a stash of mundane old objects remain. These traces support questions about the place’s former use, while the market interpretation remains an interpretation.

The small figure in the monument’s hair

Trougar finds another carving. Fenwick’s True Seeing reveals a marking beneath it, and he points out what may be a trigger. Ryvyt agrees that he should try it, ready in case the statue becomes hostile.

Instead, a tiny humanoid figure emerges among the flowers and decorations in the monument’s hair. Its words describe what Viota left behind as something the forest would not lose. It calls the Children of Viota her remembrance, rather than her descendants. The explanation belongs to the speaking figure and is later echoed in the inscription’s translation.

A shadow child watches the statue without attacking. Ryvyt calls for the company to hold, and Fenwick points out that the watcher has not struck them. Saelihn lowers Trougar’s weapon. Her belief that it has come to see its mother is a compassionate reading of the scene, not a settled family history.

Leaving the vines alive

Fenwick asks how they can help and whether an exchange over the river caused the problem. The child gives only a fragmentary answer about an earlier time, then leaves toward the dark forest. Saelihn wonders whether tending the figure could let spring return; Ryvyt proposes asking a druid.

Before leaving, Saelihn cleans the location with careful magic. She moves the vines rather than breaking them, making the monument presentable while preserving the growth around it. Fenwick copies the writing and takes the old chest back for Orin to inspect. The narrator confirms that he has copied the inscription accurately.

The company leaves with information and small recovered objects. There is no completed restoration of spring, summoned druid or later return in this closing sequence.

Ilyra’s translation

Back with Ilyra, Fenwick presents the copy. She identifies Sylvan and reads the heading: Viota of the First Passage. The inscription describes someone walking beyond autumn when spring no longer answers, a first crossing that others would not follow, and a season which cannot begin again.

Ilyra reads the same distinction the figure made: remembrance rather than descendants. Fenwick writes down the translation. The rubbing lets the company learn from the place without requiring its interpreter to have been present at the monument.

The name and words establish a history that can be investigated, rather than a complete biography of Viota. They do not identify her as a goddess, prove a living lineage, explain every shadow child in Verdelune or establish the cause of the forest’s condition. The monument remains a place whose visitors chose observation, restraint and care while its central question stayed open.
sources: Quest-RP continuation — supplied 11 Oct 2026; 2,369 messages, main quest-rp and Pristinia Library; posting dates, not in-world dates
